h3.q: Why Uber maps the world in hexagons
h3.title: Why Uber maps the world in hexagons

story.md: Picture a busy Friday night. Thousands of riders open the app while drivers cruise around the city. Uber wants to know, **neighbourhood by neighbourhood**, whether there are more riders than drivers. That balance of **supply and demand** drives things like **dynamic pricing**.

story.plain: Changing a price up or down depending on how many people want something versus how much is available.
story.like: Umbrellas costing more the moment it starts pouring.

story.md: To count things per neighbourhood, you first need neighbourhoods. You have to chop the whole Earth into cells, drop every rider and driver into a cell, and quickly answer "what's *nearby*?"

Use **square** cells, like graph paper. It's easy to code, but "nearby" gets lopsided. A square has 4 neighbours that share an edge, and 4 more that touch only at a corner. The corner ones are about 1.41 times farther from the centre. Ask for "everything one cell away" and you quietly include some neighbours that are much farther away than others.

Think of a honeycomb. Every cell touches exactly **6 neighbours**, and every one of them is the **same distance** from the centre. There are no awkward corners, and the cells tile with no gaps. Uber built and open-sourced **H3** (2018), a hierarchical hexagonal grid that covers the Earth with 16 resolutions, from big cells to small ones.

story.like: Street and avenue numbers, but for a honeycomb.

story.md: Our toy version below uses axial coordinates on a flat plane, not real latitude and longitude. It still shows the key trick. We **bucket** each driver under their cell, then answer "who's nearby?" by looking in just a handful of cells instead of checking everyone.

story.md: The [[6-8|distance function]] is the heart of the hex grid. Each cell is named `(q, r)`, and the largest of three differences gives the number of steps between any two cells. The [[24|obvious scan]] applies it to all 40 drivers, one by one. Fine for 40, but a real city has far more.

The clever way [[25-27|files each driver under their cell]] once. Then [[28-29|the ring]] lists the 19 cells within 2 steps of the rider, and we open only those buckets. Both paths give the same answer, as the final table shows. The two bar charts at [[38-39|the neighbour distances]] show the fairness: squares give two different distances, hexes give one.

Hexagons cost you simplicity. Square grids map neatly onto screens, arrays and images, while hex grids need odd coordinate systems like `(q, r)` and fiddly drawing code. Hexagons also can't nest perfectly inside bigger hexagons the way squares nest in squares, which matters for a hierarchy of resolutions. If your data is already pixels or a spreadsheet, or you only need rough counts, squares are simpler and good enough.

Any place that asks "what's near this?" over a map can use the idea: bucket first, then look up neighbours. The real thing is Uber's open-source H3, written in C with bindings for many languages. Read it at **github.com/uber/h3**.

story.q: Why does a hex grid make "everything one step away" fairer than a square grid?
choices: Hexagons are bigger than squares
All 6 neighbours are the same distance from the centre
Hexagons need fewer coordinates
story.why: A square has edge neighbours and corner neighbours at different distances (1 vs about 1.41). A hexagon's 6 neighbours are all equally far.

import math, random
random.seed(7)
S, K = 14, 2
DIRS = [(1,0),(1,-1),(0,-1),(-1,0),(-1,1),(0,1)]

def dist(a, b):
    dq, dr = a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1]
    return max(abs(dq), abs(dr), abs(dq+dr))

def px(c):
    return 200 + S*math.sqrt(3)*(c[0]+c[1]/2), 200 + S*1.5*c[1]

def draw_hex(c, color):
    x, y = px(c)
    circle(x, y, S*0.87, color)
    for i in range(6):
        a, b = math.radians(60*i-30), math.radians(60*i+30)
        line(x+S*math.cos(a), y+S*math.sin(a), x+S*math.cos(b), y+S*math.sin(b), "#222", 1)

cells = [(q, r) for q in range(-6, 7) for r in range(-6, 7) if dist((q, r), (0, 0)) <= 6]
drivers = random.choices(cells, k=40)
rider = (1, -1)

scan = [d for d in drivers if dist(d, rider) <= K]
buckets = {}
for d in drivers:
    buckets.setdefault(d, []).append(d)
ring = [(rider[0]+q, rider[1]+r) for q in range(-K, K+1) for r in range(-K, K+1) if dist((q, r), (0, 0)) <= K]
near = [d for c in ring for d in buckets.get(c, [])]

size(400, 400)
background("#111")
for c in cells:
    draw_hex(c, "#e63946" if c == rider else "#f4a261" if c in ring else "#2b2d42")
for d in drivers:
    circle(*px(d), 3, "white")

square = sorted(round(math.hypot(a, b), 2) for a in (-1, 0, 1) for b in (-1, 0, 1) if (a, b) != (0, 0))
hexes = sorted(round(math.dist(px(n), px((0, 0))) / (S*math.sqrt(3)), 2) for n in DIRS)
show(square, "square: 8 neighbours, 2 distances")
show(hexes, "hex: 6 neighbours, 1 distance")
show({"scan checks": len(drivers), "cell lookups": len(ring), "same answer": sorted(scan) == sorted(near)}, "two ways, one answer")

pagerank.q: PageRank: how Google decided which page matters
pagerank.title: PageRank: how Google decided which page matters

story.md: In 1998, Larry Page and Sergey Brin (with Motwani and Winograd) were at Stanford staring at the web. Millions of pages, and you type two words. Thousands match. Which one goes at the top?
Matching words isn't enough, because anyone can write a page full of the right words. They needed a signal the page's author couldn't easily fake: what *the rest of the web* thinks of it.

Count incoming links: each link is a vote, most votes wins. It breaks fast. Votes aren't equal: a link from a respected site means more than a link from an empty page someone made last night. Make 1,000 throwaway pages that all link to yours and you "win" the count.

Imagine someone clicking around the web forever, never reading, just following random links. Pages with lots of traffic from busy pages get visited often. Pages only reachable from dead-end corners get visited rarely. Importance becomes: *how much time does this wanderer spend here?*

Page and Brin called this wanderer the **random surfer**. One twist: sometimes the surfer gets bored and jumps to a random page instead (about 15% of the time). That keeps them from getting stuck in a loop of pages forever.

story.like: A tourist wandering a city, taking any street they see.

story.like: The odds you keep reading instead of getting bored and switching.

story.md: We don't need to simulate the surfer for years. A page's rank is the long-run share of time spent there, and we can find it with **power iteration**: start everyone equal, then repeatedly have each page hand its rank out along its links until the numbers settle.
The web is a plain dict: each page maps to the pages it links to. The [[14-17|naive count]] walks every link and adds one to its target. Spam wins with 3; Gem gets just 1.

The real work is the [[22-29|round loop]]. Each round, every page [[25-27|splits its rank among its links]] and the targets collect it. Since Wiki is important and links *only* to Gem, Gem inherits most of it. Meanwhile the fans have no inbound links, so [[31|the printed change]] drops toward zero as the numbers settle, and Spam's three votes carry almost nothing.
Compare the two charts: Gem has the fewest links among the top contenders yet ranks near the top, and Spam falls to the middle of the pack. Same web, very different verdicts.

PageRank needs the whole link graph, and every round touches every link, so it's costly on a huge web. It also says nothing about your *query*: it's a global importance score, so it can't tell which page best answers your question. Modern Google uses many more signals, so treat this as one ingredient, not the whole recipe.

Any time you want to rank things in a network by who points to them, the same "importance flows along connections" idea applies: citations between papers, followers between accounts, or links between your own notes.

hll.q: How Reddit counts views without remembering every viewer
hll.title: How Reddit counts views without remembering every viewer

story.md: Reddit wants to show how many **unique** people viewed each post. If you refresh a post five times, that's still one view. So the counter has to know whether it has seen you before, and it has to do that for every post at once.
Reddit's 2017 post "View Counting at Reddit" describes solving this with **HyperLogLog** (HLL), stored in Redis. The surprise is that it never stores who the viewers were.

Keep a **set** of every viewer id per post. Adding an id twice changes nothing, so `len(set)` is the exact unique count. The catch is memory: the set grows in proportion to the number of unique viewers. A hugely popular post needs a hugely big set, and every post needs its own.

Imagine flipping a coin until you get heads, and bragging about your longest streak of tails. If someone says "I once got 10 tails in a row," you'd guess they flipped a *lot* of times. A long streak is rare, so it hints at lots of attempts.

HLL does this with numbers. It turns each viewer id into a random-looking number with a **hash function**, then splits the hashes across a few **buckets**. Each bucket remembers only one thing: its longest run of leading zeros. Seeing the same viewer twice gives the same hash, so repeats change nothing.

story.plain: A recipe that turns any input into a fixed-size, scrambled-looking number, always giving the same number for the same input.
story.like: A blender: same fruit in, same smoothie out.

story.plain: The zeros at the start of a number written in binary, before the first 1 appears.
story.like: Tails in a row before your first heads.

story.md: Look at [[16-19|the add method]]. The hash is split in two: the top 6 bits choose one of 64 buckets, and the remaining bits are checked for leading zeros. The register only ever goes up, via `max`, so a viewer who returns just recomputes the same value.

Then [[22-23|the formula]] turns 64 small numbers into one estimate. Run it: [[35|the bar chart]] shows exact and estimated counts landing close together. The last chart, from [[37|the memory line]], compares a set that grew with every viewer to 64 registers that never grew. The set size is approximate, since `getsizeof` doesn't count the strings inside it.

You pay with accuracy: the answer is an **estimate**, not the truth, and you can't ask "did user X view this?" or list the viewers. Our 64 registers are rough. Redis HLLs use about 12 KB with a standard error around 0.81%. Don't use HLL when you need exact numbers, such as billing, or when you need to look up individuals.
Any "how many distinct X?" question at scale, such as unique visitors or distinct search queries, is a candidate. Redis ships HLL as a built-in feature, which is how Reddit used it.

items: Why does more registers mean better accuracy?

hll.code:
import hashlib, math, sys

B = 6                       # 6 bits pick the bucket
M = 2 ** B                  # 64 registers

def h(item):
    d = hashlib.sha256(str(item).encode()).digest()
    return int.from_bytes(d[:8], "big")      # a 64-bit number

class HLL:
    def __init__(self):
        self.regs = [0] * M

    def add(self, item):
        x = h(item)
        bucket = x >> (64 - B)               # top bits choose the bucket
        rest = x & ((1 << (64 - B)) - 1)     # the remaining bits
        zeros = (64 - B) - rest.bit_length() # leading zeros in rest
        self.regs[bucket] = max(self.regs[bucket], zeros + 1)

    def count(self):
        z = sum(2.0 ** -r for r in self.regs)
        est = 0.709 * M * M / z
        empty = self.regs.count(0)
        if est <= 2.5 * M and empty:         # small-count correction
            est = M * math.log(M / empty)
        return round(est)

for n in (100, 1000, 10000):
    seen, hll = set(), HLL()
    for i in range(n * 3):                   # every viewer shows up 3 times
        viewer = "user" + str(i % n)
        seen.add(viewer)
        hll.add(viewer)
    show([len(seen), hll.count()], f"{n} viewers: exact vs HLL")

show([sys.getsizeof(seen), sys.getsizeof(hll.regs)], "bytes: set vs 64 registers")

figma.q: Figma multiplayer: last writer wins, per property
figma.title: Figma multiplayer: last writer wins, per property

story.md: Picture a Figma file with two people in it. Ana drags a box to the right. At the same moment, Ben recolours that same box red. Both of them expect their change to stick, and both are watching the canvas live.

Figma's 2019 post on its multiplayer technology tackles this. Edits from many people arrive at nearly the same time, and everyone must end up looking at the **same** document without anyone's work vanishing for no reason.

The simplest fix is to lock things. Ana grabs the box, so Ben has to wait. It is safe, but it feels awful: Ben can't recolour a box just because someone nudged it. Lock the whole document and it's worse, since only one person can edit at a time. That defeats the point of working together.

Think of a shared form with separate fields: name, address, phone. If you fix the phone number and I fix the address, we don't fight. Only if we both rewrite the *phone* field does someone's edit lose, and then the later one wins.

Figma does this with every object. A central **server** is the authority and decides the order of changes. Conflicts are resolved **per property**: different properties both survive, and for the same property the last value the server receives wins. Each client applies its own edits immediately, so it feels instant.

story.plain: One central computer decides the official order of changes, and everyone else follows its version.
story.like: A referee whose call is final.

story.plain: When two changes hit the same value, the one that arrives last is kept and the earlier one is overwritten.
story.like: Two people edit one sticky note; the final scribble stays.

story.plain: A data structure designed so copies edited independently can always merge to the same result, with no central referee.
story.like: Recipe cards that can always be combined without arguing.

story.md: Figma took inspiration from CRDTs but did not use a full one. Because a server already orders the changes, it could skip the extra machinery. Below, we run both rules on the same edits.

Both rules get the same edits, in the same [[11|time order]]. Rule A, [[13-15|whole-object]], builds a fresh shape from the starting copy plus the edit. When Ben's recolour lands, it rebuilds the box from `start`, so Ana's move to x=100 is wiped out even though Ben never touched `x`.

Rule B, [[16-18|per-property]], only overwrites the named keys. The box ends up at x=100 *and* red. The [[26-29|loss check]] shows what remains: Ana@3 still loses, because Ben also set the star's `x` and was later. Same property, so last writer wins.

Per-property merging is simple and cheap, but it is blunt: a lost edit just disappears, with no merge of two intentions. It also leans on the server being the authority. Don't use it for text where two people type in the same sentence, since overwriting a whole field would destroy typing.
Database fields in many apps behave this way: two people editing different columns of one row don't clobber each other. CRDTs take the idea further when there is no central server to order things.

diff.q: How GitHub knows exactly which lines you changed
diff.title: How GitHub knows exactly which lines you changed

story.md: You open a pull request. GitHub shows a wall of grey, a few **green** lines for additions and a few **red** ones for deletions. You added one line near the top of a file, but the page doesn't claim you rewrote the whole thing. It points at just the lines that changed.

A computer has no idea what you meant. It gets two blobs of text, before and after, and must work out the smallest set of edits that turns one into the other. That list of edits is what we call a **diff**.

Compare line 1 to line 1, line 2 to line 2, and so on, flagging every mismatch. It works until someone inserts one line near the top. Now every old line sits one position lower than it used to, so *every* position mismatches, and the diff reports a total rewrite even though almost nothing changed.

Think of two people reading the same poem from different printings. Instead of matching page numbers, they hunt for the lines both versions share, in the same order, and tick them off. Whatever isn't ticked in the old copy was deleted, and whatever isn't ticked in the new copy was added.

The biggest set of lines you can tick off is called the **longest common subsequence**. Finding it is the same problem as finding the fewest edits, and Eugene Myers' 1986 paper "An O(ND) Difference Algorithm" is the approach behind Git's default diff.

story.md: The naive version, [[4-14|the first function]], only ever asks "are these two lines equal at this index?". After the inserted "a poem:" line, every comparison is off by one, so it flags six changed lines.

The clever version first fills [[16-24|a table]]. Cell `t[i][j]` holds how many lines the old text from `i` onward shares with the new text from `j` onward. [[26-40|The walk]] then follows the table from the top corner: matching lines are kept, and at a mismatch it takes whichever step keeps the shared count highest. The result is four changed lines: one added, two removed, one added back as the edit.

This table has one cell per pair of lines, so its work and memory grow with the *product* of the two lengths. That's fine for a poem and wasteful for huge files. Myers' O(ND) algorithm is built around D, the number of differences, so it is fast when files are similar. Git also offers `patience` and `histogram` diffs, which can read better in some cases.
The same idea powers `git diff` in your terminal, merge tools that compare versions, and any "track changes" view that highlights what moved between two drafts.

mapreduce.title: MapReduce: how Google counted the whole web

story.md: Picture a library with more pages than any person could read in a lifetime, and you need to know how often every word appears. Google faced this kind of job: huge datasets, far too big for one computer.
In 2004, Jeffrey Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat described how Google handled it in "MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters". Their answer used thousands of machines working together.

Put one computer in charge and have it read every page, keeping a tally of each word. It works on 12 pages. On a giant dataset it breaks twice: the data won't fit, and reading it all one page at a time takes forever. Buying a faster computer only delays the wall. Using many computers helps, but then you must split the work, collect the results, and cope with machines that die mid-job.

Imagine 1,000 students counting words in a pile of books. You hand each student a few pages. Each writes a slip for every word they see: "cat, 1". That's the **map** step. Then slips are sorted into boxes, one box per word. That's the **shuffle**. Finally one person per box adds up the slips, which is the **reduce** step.

story.md: The framework does the boring, hard parts: **splitting** the input, **scheduling** work onto machines, and **retrying** work when a machine fails. You only write the map and reduce functions.

[[10-11|Map]] turns "the cat sat" into three pairs: (the,1), (cat,1), (sat,1). The obvious way [[23|runs it on all 12 pages]] in one place. The clever way [[28-32|gives each of 4 machines 3 pages]] and has each map only its own chunk.

Then [[13-17|shuffle]] gathers the 1s into one pile per word and [[19-20|reduce]] sums each pile. The [[37|bar chart]] shows the win: one machine does 65 steps, while each of the four does at most 17. Both ways give the same counts, and "the" tops the table.

Splitting work isn't free. The shuffle moves data between machines, and the framework has to schedule and retry work. If your data fits comfortably on one computer, a plain loop is simpler and often faster. MapReduce also fits best when the job can be phrased as map, group by key, reduce.
Hadoop is a well-known open-source implementation of the same idea. The map-then-combine shape also shows up everywhere in everyday code, such as Python's list comprehensions and `sum`.

chaos.q: Why Netflix breaks its own servers on purpose
chaos.title: Why Netflix breaks its own servers on purpose

story.md: Around 2010–2011, Netflix was moving to the cloud. There, a server (an **instance**) is not a precious machine in your basement. It can simply vanish, at any moment, with no warning.
Picture millions of people pressing play while some of those machines quietly disappear. If one missing machine can break the show, you will get paged on a Friday night.

Build one good server, hope it never dies, and promise to fix it fast when it does. The trouble: you only learn whether your system survives a failure *during* a real failure, at the worst time. Code that handles failure but has never been tested is just a guess.

Think of a fire drill. You don't wait for a real fire to find out the exit is blocked, you pull the alarm on a Tuesday morning when everyone is awake. Netflix built **Chaos Monkey**, which randomly shuts down server instances in production, during business hours, when engineers are around to react.

story.plain: A Netflix tool that randomly shuts down running servers so engineers find weak spots before customers do.
story.like: A fire drill for your servers.

story.md: The deal changes. Since any server can die any minute, engineers must build services that survive it, using **redundancy** (several copies), retries, and fallbacks. The practice is now called **chaos engineering**.

story.plain: Keeping extra copies of something important, so losing one copy doesn't stop the whole system.
story.like: Carrying a spare tire in the trunk.

story.plain: A traffic director that sends each incoming request to one of several identical servers.
story.like: A host seating guests at open tables.

story.md: Both versions face the same attack: [[11-12|the monkey]] kills a random server about 5% of the time and keeps it down for 30 requests. With one server, that kill is a long outage. A fresh kill lands every ~20 requests, so the server is down much of the time.

In version B, [[13-18|the retry loop]] acts as a simple **load balancer**. It tries replicas in random order and settles for the first live one. A request only fails if all three are down at once, which is rare. Compare [[24-25|the two runs]] in the bars, then scan the grids: A fills with X runs, while B's X marks are scarce.

Redundancy costs money (three servers instead of one) and complexity (retries, health checks, data that must stay in sync). Chaos testing is risky if you have no safety net yet. Don't unleash a monkey on a system with a single server and no fallback. Build the safety first, then test it, and start small.

Netflix described this in its 2011 post "The Netflix Simian Army" and open-sourced Chaos Monkey in 2012. You can read the real thing at github.com/Netflix/chaosmonkey. Today, retries, replicas, and failure drills show up in databases, payment systems, and any app that can't afford to go down.

import random
random.seed(7)

REQUESTS, KILL_CHANCE, REPAIR_TIME = 1000, 0.05, 30

def simulate(replicas, retry):
    down = [0] * replicas      # ticks left until each server is back
    wins, log = 0, []
    for _ in range(REQUESTS):
        down = [max(0, t - 1) for t in down]
        if random.random() < KILL_CHANCE:
            down[random.randrange(replicas)] = REPAIR_TIME
        tries = random.sample(range(replicas), replicas if retry else 1)
        served = "X"
        for r in tries:
            if down[r] == 0:
                served = r
                break
        if served != "X":
            wins += 1
        log.append(served)
    return wins, log

a_wins, a_log = simulate(1, retry=False)
b_wins, b_log = simulate(3, retry=True)

show([a_wins, b_wins], "successes out of 1000: A (one server) vs B (3 replicas + retry)")
show([a_log[i:i+10] for i in range(0, 40, 10)], "A: first 40 requests (X = failed)")
show([b_log[i:i+10] for i in range(0, 40, 10)], "B: first 40 requests (number = replica)")

bloom.q: How Chrome checked millions of bad links without downloading them
bloom.title: How Chrome checked millions of bad links without downloading them

story.md: You click a link. Before the page loads, your browser should know whether it's a known phishing or malware site. The list of known-bad URLs is huge and keeps changing.
Asking Google's servers about **every** link would be slow, and it would mean telling a server every page you visit. Chrome's Safe Browsing wanted to answer most checks locally, on your own machine.

Ship the browser a plain list of every bad URL and look each link up. It works, but every URL is a long string, so the list grows with the number of bad sites. Millions of strings means a big download, big memory use, and constant updates, all on your laptop or phone.

Picture a wall of light switches, all off. To remember a bad URL, you don't write it down. You run it through three scrambling machines, and each one tells you a switch to flip on. To check a new URL, run the same three machines: if **all three** switches are on, it's *maybe* bad. If even one is off, it's definitely not on the list.

story.plain: A small array of bits that remembers a set, answering 'definitely not in it' or 'probably in it'.
story.like: A wall of switches that remembers fingerprints, not the names.

story.plain: A recipe that turns any text into a number, always the same number for the same text.
story.like: A blender that always makes the same smoothie from the same fruit.

story.like: A smoke alarm going off over burnt toast.

story.md: Different URLs can accidentally flip overlapping switches, which is where false positives come from. But a bad URL always flips its own three, so the filter never misses one (no **false negatives**). On a "maybe", Chrome asks Google's servers to be sure. Burton Bloom invented this in 1970.

[[9-10|The hash step]] turns a URL into three positions between 0 and 511. [[12-14|Adding]] a URL just switches those three bits on, and [[16-17|checking]] asks whether all three are on. Nothing about the URL itself is stored.

Run it and look at [[34|the grid]]: the lit cells are the filter's whole memory. Then compare [[27|the exact list]], which finds no false alarms, with [[28|the filter]], which may flag a few good URLs. The last bar chart shows what that buys: 512 bits against thousands for the raw strings.

You pay with certainty: false positives happen, and the more items you add to a fixed array, the more bits are on and the more often they happen. You can't list what's inside, and you can't easily remove an item, since its bits may be shared. Don't use one when a wrong 'yes' is costly and there's no cheap way to double-check.

Databases like Apache Cassandra and Google Bigtable use Bloom filters to skip disk reads for keys that aren't there. A quick 'definitely not' saves a slow trip to disk, the same way it saved Chrome a trip to the server.

import hashlib
import random

M, K = 512, 3  # bits in the filter, number of hash functions
bits = [0] * M

def spots(url):
    # K positions in the bit array for this URL
    return [int(hashlib.sha256(f"{i}:{url}".encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % M
            for i in range(K)]

def add(url):
    for s in spots(url):
        bits[s] = 1

def maybe_bad(url):
    return all(bits[s] for s in spots(url))

random.seed(7)
bad = [f"evil{n}.example/login" for n in range(50)]
good = [f"site{random.randint(0, 10**6)}.example/home" for _ in range(200)]

for url in bad:
    add(url)

# obvious way: scan the full list of strings
exact = sum(u in bad for u in good)
fooled = sum(maybe_bad(u) for u in good)
missed = sum(not maybe_bad(u) for u in bad)

print("Obvious list false alarms:", exact)
print("Bloom false positives:", fooled, "of 200")
print("Bloom misses of real bad URLs:", missed)
show([bits[r*32:(r+1)*32] for r in range(M // 32)], "Bloom bit array")
list_bits = sum(len(u) for u in bad) * 8
show([list_bits, M], "bits used: full list vs Bloom filter")

snowflake.title: Snowflake: Twitter's IDs that tell time

story.md: Every tweet needs its own ID, and no two tweets can ever share one. By 2010 Twitter was storing tweets on **many machines at once**, and all of them were creating new records at the same moment.
So Twitter announced **Snowflake**: a way to make unique 64-bit IDs across many machines *without* the machines talking to each other. As a bonus, the IDs sort roughly by time.

Keep one shared counter. Need an ID? Ask the counter for the next number. This works on one machine. With many machines, they all queue at that single counter, and a **lock** makes them take turns. If the counter is slow or down, nobody can make IDs. The code below runs this version too, so you can see it.
Think of a coat-check ticket that reads *"Tuesday, 14:03:07, desk 2, ticket 5"*. Two desks can never clash, because the desk number is baked into the ticket. And nobody had to phone a central office.

Snowflake packs one 64-bit number the same way: 1 unused sign bit, then 41 bits of **milliseconds since a custom epoch**, then 10 bits of machine (worker) id, then 12 bits of a per-millisecond sequence number. Time goes first, so newer IDs are bigger.

story.plain: Machines messaging each other to agree on something before they act.
story.like: Calling the head office before every single sale.

story.plain: The starting moment you count time from, so the numbers stay small.

story.plain: A small counter that separates IDs made by one worker in the same millisecond.

EPOCH = 1_700_000_000_000  # our own demo start time (ms)

class Snowflake:
    def __init__(self, worker):
        self.worker = worker
        self.last_ms = -1
        self.seq = 0

    def next_id(self, now_ms):
        if now_ms == self.last_ms:
            self.seq += 1
        else:
            self.last_ms, self.seq = now_ms, 0
        return ((now_ms - EPOCH) << 22) | (self.worker << 12) | self.seq

def decode(i):
    return [i, i >> 22, (i >> 12) & 1023, i & 4095]

# Obvious way: ONE shared counter. Every machine must ask it, and a lock
# makes them take turns so nobody gets the same number twice.
counter, trips = 0, 0
def locked_next():
    global counter, trips
    trips += 1      # a network trip to the single central counter
    counter += 1    # imagine a lock held around this line
    return counter

workers = [Snowflake(w) for w in (1, 2, 3)]
ids = []
for step in range(12):
    now = EPOCH + 1000 + step // 6 * 5   # fake clock: 5 ms per round
    ids.append(workers[step % 3].next_id(now))
    locked_next()

show([["id", "ms", "worker", "seq"]] + [decode(i) for i in ids[:6]], "Decoded IDs")
show([sum(decode(i)[2] == w for i in ids) for w in (1, 2, 3)], "IDs per worker")
show({"counter: trips to central": trips, "snowflake: trips to central": 0,
      "all unique": len(set(ids)) == 12,

merkle.q: Git’s secret: every file is named by its fingerprint
merkle.title: Git's secret: every file is named by its fingerprint

story.md: Git (Linus Torvalds, 2005) has to track whole projects: thousands of files in nested folders, snapshotted again and again. Every time you commit, Git must answer: **what changed since last time?**
It also must not waste space. If a thousand snapshots contain the same unchanged file, Git shouldn't keep a thousand copies.

Compare the two snapshots file by file, byte by byte. It works, but the cost grows with the *size of the whole project*, even if you edited a single comma. A project with 120 files means 120 comparisons to find one edit. A huge project means a huge wait for a tiny change.

Imagine every file wears a name tag that is a **fingerprint** of its contents. Change one letter and the tag changes completely. Now a folder gets a tag too, made from the tags of everything inside it. Two folders with the same tag must hold identical stuff, so you can skip them without opening anything.

That's Git. Each file (a **blob**) is stored under the SHA-1 hash of its contents. Each folder (a **tree**) lists its children's hashes, so its own hash depends on everything inside. A commit points to the top tree. Identical files get the same name, so they're stored only once.

story.like: A fingerprint: tiny, but unique to its owner.

story.md: [[6-11|build]] works bottom-up. A file's hash comes straight from its text ([[8|this line]]). A folder first hashes its children, then hashes their names and fingerprints glued together. That's why editing one file changes its folder's hash and the root's hash, and nothing else.

[[13-22|walk]] compares two snapshots top-down. At every node it asks one question: [[15|do the hashes match?]] If yes, the whole subtree is skipped. Here that means the root, then `dir3`, then only its 20 files: 27 comparisons, against [[38|120 for the brute-force loop]]. Both ways report the same changed file, but one never looked at five of the six folders.

Hashing isn't free: you must read every byte once to compute a fingerprint, and any change forces re-hashing the path from that file up to the root. It also assumes two different contents never share a hash, which is why Git is moving to SHA-256 as an option. If you compare just once and never again, or the data is tiny, simply comparing directly is simpler and just as fast.
Merkle trees also appear in file-sync tools, databases that compare replicas, and blockchains. To see the real thing, browse the source at github.com/git/git.

recs.title: People like you also liked: the idea behind Netflix-style picks

story.md: Open a streaming app and you face a huge catalogue and a few seconds of patience. Nobody can browse it all. The service has to guess which few titles you'd enjoy, and it has to guess for each member separately.

Netflix cared enough about this to run the **Netflix Prize** (2006–2009): a $1M competition to improve its rating predictions by 10%. Predicting what you'd rate a title you haven't seen was the core puzzle.

Just recommend whatever is most popular: average everyone's ratings and show the top title. It's easy, and it works for nobody in particular. A sci-fi fan gets the romance everyone else loved, because the average has no idea who is asking.

Think of asking a friend for a movie tip. You don't poll the whole town. You ask the friend whose taste matches yours, the one who loved the same films you did. Now do that with math: find members whose past ratings look like yours, then borrow their opinions about what you haven't seen.

story.plain: Recommending items to you based on what people with tastes similar to yours liked.
story.like: Asking the friend who always shares your taste.

story.md: To measure "similar taste" we treat each person's ratings as an arrow and check whether two arrows point the same way. That score is **cosine similarity**: near 1 means alike, near 0 means unrelated.

story.plain: A score from 0 to 1 for how closely two lists of ratings point in the same direction.
story.like: Two compasses pointing the same way, however far apart.

story.md: Maya loves space and robots and dislikes romance. [[15-22|The cosine function]] gives Ben and Cleo scores near 1 for her, and Dev, Eli and Fay (romance and comedy fans) much lower ones. That's the "friend with your taste" step, done with numbers.

Then [[32-33|the prediction]] asks only Maya's closest twins who saw the title, and averages their ratings, weighting closer twins more. Compare it with [[27-29|the popular score]], which just averages everyone. Run it and look at [[37-38|the two charts]]: popularity picks Cold Case (3.75), while Maya's twins give Star Run about 5.

A newcomer has no ratings, so there are no twins to find (the "cold start" problem), and comparing every pair of members gets costly as they grow. The Netflix Prize shows the other side: winning approaches blended many models, notably **matrix factorisation**, yet Netflix has said it ultimately did not deploy the full winning **ensemble** because of engineering cost. Real systems use many signals, so treat this as one ingredient.

import math

titles = ["Space Saga", "Star Run", "Robo Pals", "Love Letters",
          "Chef Wars", "Laugh Riot", "Cold Case", "Dark Manor"]
names = ["Maya", "Ben", "Cleo", "Dev", "Eli", "Fay"]
N = None
R = [[5, N, 5, 1, N, 2, N, N],
     [5, 5, 4, 2, 1, N, 2, N],
     [4, 5, 5, N, 2, 1, N, 2],
     [1, N, 2, 5, 5, 4, 4, N],
     [2, 1, N, 5, 4, 5, 5, 3],
     [N, 2, 1, 4, 5, 5, 4, 4]]
show([[v or 0 for v in row] for row in R], "ratings (0 = unseen)")

def cosine(a, b):
    both = [(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b) if x and y]
    if not both:
        return 0
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in both)
    na = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x, _ in both))
    nb = math.sqrt(sum(y * y for _, y in both))
    return dot / (na * nb)

sims = {u: cosine(R[0], R[u]) for u in range(1, 6)}
show({names[u]: round(s, 2) for u, s in sims.items()}, "similarity to Maya")

def popular(t):
    col = [row[t] for row in R[1:] if row[t]]
    return sum(col) / len(col)

def predict(t, k=2):
    fans = sorted((u for u in sims if R[u][t]), key=lambda u: -sims[u])[:k]
    return sum(sims[u] * R[u][t] for u in fans) / sum(sims[u] for u in fans)

unseen = [t for t, v in enumerate(R[0]) if v is None]
print("Maya hasn't seen:", [titles[t] for t in unseen])
show([round(popular(t), 2) for t in unseen], "obvious: popular")
show([round(predict(t), 2) for t in unseen], "clever: people like Maya")
print("Popular pick:", titles[max(unseen, key=popular)])
print("Clever pick:", titles[max(unseen, key=predict)])

shazam.q: How Shazam names a song from ten noisy seconds
shazam.title: How Shazam names a song from ten noisy seconds

story.md: You're in a loud bar. A song comes on, you hold up your phone, and ten seconds later Shazam names it. The clip has chatter, clinking glasses and a cheap phone microphone mixed in with the music.

Shazam has to match that messy clip against a huge catalogue of clean recordings, and it has to do it fast. Avery Li-Chun Wang's 2003 paper, *An Industrial-Strength Audio Search Algorithm*, describes the method.

Compare the recording's raw samples against every song, sliding along until they line up. It breaks the moment anything differs. Noise changes nearly every sample, so the clip never equals any stretch of the original, and even a tiny mismatch ruins an exact comparison. Sliding over a whole catalogue would be slow too.

Think of recognising a friend in a crowd photo. You don't compare every pixel. You spot a few landmarks, like the tall hat next to the red scarf. Shazam turns audio into a **spectrogram**, a picture of which pitches are loud at each moment, and keeps only the strongest peaks. That sparse dot pattern is a **constellation map**. Noise rarely erases the loudest peaks, so many survive.

story.like: Sheet music drawn automatically from a recording.

story.plain: The few strongest peaks of a spectrogram, kept as (time, frequency) dots, with everything else thrown away.

story.md: Next, **pair** nearby peaks and **hash** each pair as (frequency1, frequency2, time gap). To match a clip, look up its hashes in an index. The real song gets many hits that all agree on the same time offset, while accidental hits scatter. So the app counts votes per (song, offset).

story.md: [[7-9|The hash function]] pairs every peak with peaks 1 to 3 steps later, and [[11-14|the index]] files each hash under the song and time it came from. The clip is then [[17-18|damaged on purpose]]: some peaks dropped, some noise added. Fewer than half the original pairs survive, but some do.

The [[28|obvious approach]] finds the clean clip but returns "no match" for the noisy one. The clever approach looks up each surviving hash, and [[33|the vote key]] is (song, offset). Blues collects many votes on a single offset of 20, while the other songs only get stray collisions. The bar chart shows the gap.

You pay up front: every song must be analysed and indexed, and the index takes memory. Matching also needs enough surviving peaks, so a clip that is mostly noise, or a heavily changed version like a remix at a new tempo, may not match. Don't use it to find songs that merely sound similar. It finds the same recording.
Hash an index, then vote on agreement. The same pattern shows up in near-duplicate image search and in DNA sequence matching, where messy fragments are matched against a big reference.

lru.q: How Redis decides what to forget
lru.title: How Redis decides what to forget

story.md: Redis is a **cache**: it keeps popular data in fast memory so apps don't have to fetch it from somewhere slower. But memory is finite. Eventually it fills up, and every new key that arrives forces a question: what do we throw away?

story.plain: A small, fast store holding copies of data that is likely to be asked for again.
story.like: Your desk, versus the filing cabinet down the hall.

story.md: The rule for picking a victim is called an **eviction policy**. A popular choice is **least-recently-used (LRU)**: remove the item that has gone untouched the longest. The bet is that if nobody has asked for it in ages, nobody will soon.

story.plain: The rule a full cache uses to choose which stored item to remove next.
story.like: A librarian's rule for which book leaves the shelf.

story.plain: Least-recently-used: when space runs out, remove the item that was touched longest ago.
story.like: Cleaning out the fridge, starting with what you haven't opened in ages.

story.md: Keep every key in a perfect list, ordered from most to least recently used. Each read moves that key to the front, and eviction takes the one at the back. It's exactly right, but it means tracking a full ordering of **all** keys and reshuffling it on every single access. That's extra memory and extra work spent on bookkeeping instead of serving data.

Redis documents that its LRU is **approximated**. It doesn't keep a perfect ordering. When it must evict, it **samples** a few keys (`maxmemory-samples`, default 5) and evicts the oldest one *in that sample*. Think of picking 5 random milk cartons from a huge fridge and tossing the one with the oldest date. It's not guaranteed the oldest in the fridge, but it's usually very old.

story.like: Tasting one spoonful to judge the whole pot of soup.

story.md: Redis documents this as close to true LRU at far lower memory cost. Let's check that claim ourselves: 2000 requests, 100 possible keys, a cache that holds only 20, and a few keys that are much more popular than the rest.

Both caches see the identical [[7|2000 requests]], so the contest is fair. The perfect one uses an `OrderedDict`: [[14|every hit moves the key to the end]], so [[17|the front is always the true oldest]].

The sampled one keeps no order at all, just a [[30|last-used timestamp]] per key. When full, it [[27|grabs 5 random keys]] and [[28|takes the stalest]]. Run it: the bars for exact and sampled should sit very close, and both dwarf the no-cache bar of 0.

Sampling is sometimes wrong: it can evict a key that was fairly recent because all five candidates happened to be recent too. You trade a little accuracy for less memory and less bookkeeping. If your cache is tiny, or a single wrong eviction is very costly, exact LRU is simple and may be the better choice.

The idea of *check a small random sample instead of everything* shows up across computing whenever perfect knowledge costs too much. To see how Redis really does it, browse the open-source code at github.com/redis/redis.

lru.code:
import random
from collections import OrderedDict

random.seed(7)
SIZE, REQUESTS, SAMPLES = 20, 2000, 5
weights = [1 / (k + 1) for k in range(100)]
requests = random.choices(range(100), weights, k=REQUESTS)

def exact_lru(reqs):
    cache, hits = OrderedDict(), 0
    for k in reqs:
        if k in cache:
            hits += 1
            cache.move_to_end(k)
        else:
            if len(cache) >= SIZE:
                cache.popitem(last=False)
            cache[k] = True
    return hits / len(reqs) * 100

def sampled_lru(reqs):
    last_used, hits = {}, 0
    for t, k in enumerate(reqs):
        if k in last_used:
            hits += 1
        elif len(last_used) >= SIZE:
            pool = random.sample(list(last_used), SAMPLES)
            oldest = min(pool, key=last_used.get)
            del last_used[oldest]
        last_used[k] = t
    return hits / len(reqs) * 100

exact = exact_lru(requests)
sampled = sampled_lru(requests)
show([0, round(exact, 1), round(sampled, 1)], "hit %: no cache | exact LRU | sampled (5)")
print(f"gap: {abs(exact - sampled):.1f} points")

pow.q: Bitcoin’s puzzle: making cheating too expensive
pow.title: Bitcoin's puzzle: making cheating too expensive

story.md: Picture a shared ledger with no bank in charge: "Alice pays Bob 5", "Bob pays Cy 2". Thousands of strangers keep copies. Anyone can offer a new page of transactions, and some of them would love to quietly edit an old page.
The 2008 whitepaper by Satoshi Nakamoto asks: how can strangers agree on one history, when lying is easy and nobody can be trusted? The answer is to make **rewriting the past absurdly expensive**.

Just trust whoever writes the next page first, and link pages together so edits are noticeable. The flaw: if linking is free, a cheater edits page 1, recomputes the links for every later page in a blink, and hands you a perfectly consistent fake history. Nothing slowed them down.

Think of a lottery where buying tickets is the only way to win. To add a page, a miner must find a lucky number, called a **nonce**, that makes the page's fingerprint start with enough zeros. That is **proof of work**: finding the number takes many tries, but checking it takes one.

story.md: Each block also contains the previous block's SHA-256 hash, so blocks form a chain. Change an old block and its hash changes, which breaks every later link. Rewriting history means redoing all that work. The network even adjusts difficulty every 2016 blocks to aim for about ten minutes per block.

[[8-10|The mining loop]] is the whole trick: bump the nonce, hash again, stop when the hash starts with K zeros. The first chart shows each extra zero makes mining cost far more tries. Meanwhile [[18|this line]] chains each block to the one before it.

After we edit block 1, [[24-26|the check]] flags the damaged blocks, because the edited hash no longer matches or no longer has its zeros. To hide it, a cheater must redo blocks 1 to 3. [[36-37|The two rewrites]] show the gap: with K=0 it costs 3 tries, with real work it costs thousands.

The price of security is wasted effort: honest miners also burn many tries for every block they add, and the difficulty must be retuned (every 2016 blocks in Bitcoin) to keep the pace steady. If everyone already trusts one organization, a plain database is simpler and far faster. Proof of work earns its cost only when strangers must agree without a referee.

Any system where a cheap check protects against an expensive forgery uses the same shape. The real thing lives in the open-source repository at github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin, where you can read how Bitcoin validates blocks.

import hashlib

def digest(b):
    return hashlib.sha256(f"{b['data']}|{b['prev']}|{b['nonce']}".encode()).hexdigest()

def mine(data, prev, k):
    block, tries = {"data": data, "prev": prev, "nonce": 0}, 1
    while not digest(block).startswith("0" * k):
        block["nonce"] += 1
        tries += 1
    return block, tries

def build(datas, k):
    chain, prev, tries = [], "0" * 64, 0
    for d in datas:
        block, t = mine(d, prev, k)
        chain.append(block)
        prev, tries = digest(block), tries + t
    return chain, tries

def check(chain, k):
    rows = {}
    for i, b in enumerate(chain):
        linked = i == 0 or b["prev"] == digest(chain[i - 1])
        worked = digest(b).startswith("0" * k)
        rows[f"block {i}"] = "valid" if linked and worked else "BROKEN"
    return rows

words = ["Alice pays Bob 5", "Bob pays Cy 2", "Cy pays Dee 1", "Dee pays Al 1"]
show([build(words, k)[1] for k in (1, 2, 3, 4)], "tries to mine 4 blocks, K = 1..4")

chain, _ = build(words, 3)
chain[1]["data"] = "Bob pays Cy 200"
show(check(chain, 3), "block links after tampering")

_, obvious = build(words[1:], 0)
_, clever = build(words[1:], 3)
show([obvious, clever], "cost to rewrite blocks 1-3: no work vs work")

ring.q: The ring that lets Discord add servers without chaos
ring.title: The ring that lets Discord add servers without chaos

story.md: Discord has a huge number of guilds (what you call servers), and each guild's live state has to be handled by exactly one process at a time. Every message, join and presence update for that guild must be routed to its one owner.

Then the fleet changes: you add a machine for growth, or one dies. If every guild suddenly needs a new owner, that's a stampede of handoffs. Discord has written about routing guilds to processes with a **hash ring** to avoid exactly that.

The first idea is `hash(key) % number_of_servers`. It's simple and spreads keys evenly. But the answer depends on the server count, so going from 4 to 5 servers changes the divisor for **every** key. Most keys land on a different server, and each one has to move.

story.md: Picture a clock face. Hash each server to a spot on the clock. Hash each key to a spot too. A key belongs to the first server you meet walking **clockwise** from it, like a bus stop served by the next bus that arrives.

Add a new bus and it takes over only the stops just before it. Everyone else keeps their bus. This is **consistent hashing**, popularised by the 1997 Karger et al. paper and used in Amazon's Dynamo paper (2007). Dynamo also uses **virtual nodes**: each server gets many spots on the ring so the load evens out.

Distributed caches, databases and load balancers use the same trick; Dynamo is the famous example. To read a production-grade version, Discord open-sourced an Elixir hash ring library: **github.com/discord/ex_hash_ring**.

bucket.title: Stripe's token bucket: saying "slow down" politely

story.md: Picture Stripe's API on a busy day. Thousands of programs are asking it to charge cards, and one of them has a bug that loops and fires requests as fast as it can. Without protection, that single user could slow things down for everyone else.

Stripe's 2017 post, "Scaling your API with rate limiters", describes the fix: a **rate limiter** that gives each user a budget. Go over it and the API refuses with an **HTTP 429** ("too many requests") instead of melting.

story.md: Count requests in a **fixed window**: allow 10 per 5 seconds, and reset the count to zero when a new window starts. It's simple, but it has a hole at the edges. Send 10 requests in the last instant of one window and 10 more in the first instant of the next. The counter never complains, yet 20 requests landed within a fraction of a second, double the limit. Stripe's post points out this same weakness.

Give every user a bucket of tokens. Think of a arcade with a jar of tokens: each game costs one token, and an attendant drops new tokens in at a steady pace. The jar can only hold so many. Empty jar? You wait.

That is the **token bucket**. It has a maximum size, refills at a steady rate, and every request spends one token. Stripe described building it on Redis, a fast shared store. Because a full bucket can be spent all at once, it allows a short **burst**, while the refill rate enforces the average.

story.md: Both limiters see the same traffic from [[4-5|these two lines]]: a burst straddling the 5-second mark, then a hammering spree. The fixed window in [[20-22|its counting lines]] files each request into window 0 (0–5s) or window 1 (5–10s). Each window has its own count, so both bursts of 10 pass, giving 20 in 0.2 seconds.

The bucket works differently. [[10|The refill line]] adds `(t - last) * RATE` tokens, so after 0.2 seconds it has gained only 0.4 of a token. The first burst [[12-14|spends]] all 10 tokens, and the second finds an almost empty jar. Compare the two bar charts: the window has two tall bars side by side, while the bucket has one. During the hammering at 30s, the bucket also keeps letting a request through whenever a token trickles in.

A token bucket needs a little state per user (tokens and last-seen time) that must be shared across every server, which is why Stripe used Redis. It also allows bursts by design, so skip it if you need a hard "never more than N in any instant" rule, or if the extra state isn't worth it for a tiny internal tool, where a plain counter may be fine.
Any API that returns 429s is likely using a token bucket or a close cousin. Network routers use the same idea to shape traffic, and game servers use it to stop spammy clients.

CAP, RATE = 10, 2          # bucket size, tokens per second
LIMIT, WINDOW = 10, 5      # fixed window: 10 per 5 seconds

requests = [4.9] * 10 + [5.1] * 10               # burst across a window edge
requests += [30 + i * 0.05 for i in range(40)]   # then 2s of hammering

def token_bucket(times):
    tokens, last, ok = CAP, 0, []
    for t in times:
        tokens = min(CAP, tokens + (t - last) * RATE)
        last = t
        if tokens >= 1:
            tokens -= 1
            ok.append(t)
    return ok

def fixed_window(times):
    counts, ok = {}, []
    for t in times:
        w = int(t // WINDOW)
        if counts.get(w, 0) < LIMIT:
            counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
            ok.append(t)
    return ok

def per_second(ok):
    return [sum(1 for t in ok if int(t) == s) for s in range(60)]

bucket, window = token_bucket(requests), fixed_window(requests)
show(per_second(window), "fixed window: allowed per second")
show(per_second(bucket), "token bucket: allowed per second")

print("Let through between 4.9s and 5.1s:")
print("  fixed window:", edge(window))
print("  token bucket:", edge(bucket))

astar.q: A*: how a map app finds your route without trying them all
astar.title: A*: how a map app finds your route without trying them all

story.md: You type "home" into a map app and want directions to a place far away. The road network is a huge web of intersections joined by road segments. Somewhere in that web is the quickest route, and you expect it in a blink.

Navigation software builds on **shortest-path search**. The trouble is scale: a continent has an enormous number of intersections, and millions of people ask for routes all the time. Checking every possible route is hopeless.

story.plain: Finding the cheapest chain of steps between two points in a network, where each step has a cost.
story.like: Picking the quickest chain of hops between two train stations.

story.md: The classic answer is **Dijkstra's algorithm**. It always expands the closest unexplored place next, so it spreads out like a ripple in a pond, evenly in every direction. It is correct, but it has no sense of direction. If you're heading east, it still carefully explores west, north and south, until the ripple finally reaches your goal.

story.plain: A search that always visits the unexplored place with the smallest total distance from the start.
story.like: A ripple spreading evenly from where a pebble lands.

story.md: Imagine walking through a city toward a tower you can see on the skyline. You don't check every street equally. You favor the streets that point at the tower. That is **A\*** (Hart, Nilsson and Raphael, 1968): Dijkstra plus a guess about how far is left.

Each place is ranked by *distance already traveled* plus a **heuristic**, a cheap estimate of the distance remaining. On a grid, the **Manhattan distance** (steps across plus steps down) works well. Places that look closer to the goal get explored first, so the search leans toward the goal instead of rippling everywhere.

import heapq

W, H, C = 20, 14, 14
walls = {(9, y) for y in range(2, 12)} | {(14, y) for y in range(4, 14)}
start, goal = (1, 6), (18, 6)

def search(use_h):
    h = lambda c: abs(c[0]-goal[0]) + abs(c[1]-goal[1]) if use_h else 0
    best, came, seen = {start: 0}, {}, []
    queue = [(h(start), 0, start)]
    while queue:
        _, g, cell = heapq.heappop(queue)
        if g > best[cell]: continue
        seen.append(cell)
        if cell == goal: break
        x, y = cell
        for nxt in [(x+1, y), (x-1, y), (x, y+1), (x, y-1)]:
            ok = 0 <= nxt[0] < W and 0 <= nxt[1] < H and nxt not in walls
            if ok and g + 1 < best.get(nxt, 999):
                best[nxt], came[nxt] = g + 1, cell
                heapq.heappush(queue, (g + 1 + h(nxt), g + 1, nxt))
    path = [goal]
    while path[-1] != start:
        path.append(came[path[-1]])
    return seen, path

def draw(seen, path, ox):
    for x in range(W):
        for y in range(H):
            rect(ox + x*C, y*C, C-1, C-1, "#2b2d42" if (x, y) in walls else "#f1f3f5")
    for x, y in seen: rect(ox + x*C, y*C, C-1, C-1, "#a5d8ff")
    for x, y in path: rect(ox + x*C, y*C, C-1, C-1, "#ff922b")

idem.q: Idempotency keys: how Stripe avoids charging you twice
idem.title: Idempotency keys: how Stripe avoids charging you twice

story.md: You tap **Pay** on a shop's checkout page. The shop's server calls Stripe's API, Stripe charges the card, and the reply starts travelling back... and the network drops it. The shop never hears "success".

Now the shop is stuck with a question it cannot answer: *did the charge happen or not?* Networks fail in the middle all the time, and with money on the line, a wrong guess means either a lost sale or a customer billed twice.

The obvious fix is to try again until you get an answer. That works for reading a web page, but a payment is different. If the first charge went through and only the *reply* was lost, the retry is a brand-new request, and the server happily charges the card a second time. The more flaky the network, the more double charges.

Think of a coat check. You hand over a coat and get a numbered ticket. If you come back and say "ticket 17, please" twice, they don't give you two coats, they point at the same coat. Stripe's 2017 post on idempotency describes the same trick: the client attaches a unique **idempotency key** to the request, in an `Idempotency-Key` header.

story.plain: A unique label the client puts on a request so the server can recognise a repeat of the same request.
story.like: Like a coat-check ticket number.

story.md: The server does the work once and stores the result under that key. If the same key shows up again, it skips the work and returns the saved result. An operation that gives the same outcome no matter how many times you send it is called **idempotent**. Pair this with retries that wait longer each time (**exponential backoff**) plus a random wiggle (**jitter**), and a flaky network becomes safe for payments.

Client B [[27|makes one key per order]] and reuses it on every retry. When a retry arrives, [[8|the server finds the key]] and replays the saved answer instead of charging. You don't need this for requests that are already safe to repeat, like reading data, and backoff makes a client slower to finish when the network is bad.

Anywhere a repeat is costly: sending an order, booking a seat, submitting a form, or a message queue delivering the same job twice. The pattern is always the same: label the request, remember the answer, replay it.

shuffle.q: Why Spotify made shuffle less random
shuffle.title: Why Spotify made shuffle less random

story.md: Imagine you hit shuffle on a playlist and hear three songs in a row by the same artist. You'd think the app was broken. In 2014, Spotify engineer Lukáš Poláček wrote in the post "How to shuffle songs?" that listeners were complaining exactly this: shuffle didn't feel random.
The twist is that the shuffle was fine. Truly random orders often **clump** songs by the same artist, and people read clumps as a bug.

The standard truly-random shuffle is **Fisher–Yates**: walk the list and swap each song with a randomly chosen earlier spot. Every ordering is equally likely. That's the problem: orderings with two songs from one artist side by side are plentiful, so they show up often.

story.md: Think of hanging photos on a wall. You wouldn't throw them up at random; you'd space each series evenly. Spotify did something like that: spread each artist's songs roughly evenly across the playlist, with **random offsets** so it still feels unpredictable. The post says it was inspired by **dithering**.

Dithering-style spreading shows up in image rendering, where it avoids visible blobs of one colour, and in anywhere you want "random but evenly mixed", like rotating ads or mixing quiz questions across topics.

dh.q: How WhatsApp agrees on a secret in public
dh.title: How WhatsApp agrees on a secret in public

story.md: You send a message to a friend. It hops through cables, Wi-Fi routers and servers you will never see. To keep it private, you and your friend need to **scramble** it with a shared secret key, and nobody else may know that key.

Here is the catch. You have never met in person, so the only way to agree on the key is to talk over that same watched channel. In 2016, WhatsApp announced it had finished rolling out end-to-end encryption using the Signal Protocol, and solving this puzzle is the heart of it.

Just send the key: "Hi, our password is 77." Anyone listening on the wire now knows 77 too, and can unscramble every message you ever send. The secret was exposed at the exact moment you shared it, so the scrambling protects nothing.

Picture mixing paint. You and a friend publicly agree on a shared yellow. Each of you secretly picks a private color and mixes it in, then you swap the mixed buckets in public. Each of you adds your own private color to the other's bucket. You both end up with the same final shade, and a spy holding only the swapped buckets cannot un-mix them.

That is **Diffie–Hellman key agreement** (1976). Each side keeps a private number and sends a public value computed from it. Both then compute the same shared secret. Real Signal uses an elliptic-curve version called X25519, but the toy below shows the same shape.

story.md: The obvious way, [[9-11|lines 9–11]], is a dead end: whatever crosses the wire is the key. The clever way starts at [[14-17|the exchange]]. `pow(g, a, p)` means "g to the power a, then keep only the remainder after dividing by p". Alice sends `A`, Bob sends `B`, and each raises the other's value to their own private number to land on the same secret.

Eve's only move is [[1-4|brute force]]. With a tiny prime she finds the private number quickly. Look at [[25-28|the growth loop]]: the bars climb steeply as the prime gets bigger, because each extra bit roughly doubles her tries. Then [[20-23|the XOR step]] shows the secret doing its job, scrambling and unscrambling a message.

Key agreement costs real computation, and the toy numbers here are breakable, which is why real ones are huge. It also proves nothing about *who* you are talking to, so you still need a way to verify identity. Signal adds ratchets that keep changing the keys, so one stolen key doesn't expose everything. Don't use hand-rolled code like this for real secrets.

Variants of this idea set up secure connections all over the internet. To see the production-grade version, with X25519 and the ratchets, browse the open-source Signal library at github.com/signalapp/libsignal.

hedge.q: How Google makes slow requests rare: ask twice
hedge.title: How Google makes slow requests rare: ask twice

story.md: When you search at Google, your one request doesn't go to one computer. It **fans out** to many servers, each holding a piece of the answer, and the page is only done when the last one replies.

Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso described the catch in their 2013 paper *The Tail at Scale*. If just 1% of server calls are slow, a request touching 100 servers is slow most of the time. Rare slowness becomes the normal experience.

story.plain: The rare, very slow responses at the far end of the response-time distribution, which end up dominating big requests.
story.like: The one slow checkout line that holds up your whole group.

story.md: Ask one server, wait for its answer. It's simple, and for one call it's fine. But a page needing 100 answers is a coin you flip 100 times: each flip has a 1% chance of landing on "slow", and the page waits for the worst one. That's about a 63% chance of a slow page, even though 99% of servers are healthy.

Picture ordering coffee for a whole office. You ask one barista, and if your drink hasn't appeared after a reasonable wait, you quietly ask a second barista too. Whichever hands you a cup first wins, and you ignore the other.

That's a **hedged request**. Send to one **replica**, and if it hasn't answered within roughly the 95th **percentile** time, send a backup to another replica and use whichever answers first. The cost is a little extra load, since only the slow few trigger a backup.

lsm.q: Why Google’s LevelDB writes to a pile first
lsm.title: Why Google's LevelDB writes to a pile first

story.md: Picture a service at Google that stores a huge number of small records: one key, one value, and new ones arriving all day. Every write must be saved safely, and every key must stay findable. Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat built **LevelDB**, a key-value store that Google open-sourced in 2011, for exactly this job.

Keep one big sorted file, and put each new key in its correct spot. Lookups stay easy, but every insert pushes everything after that spot one place to the right. With 1,000 keys already stored, a key landing in the middle shifts about 500 of them. As the file grows, each write gets more expensive, and on disk those scattered rewrites are especially painful.

Think of a desk. You don't file every paper into the cabinet the moment it arrives. You toss it on a pile, and when the pile is big enough you sort it once and file the whole stack. LevelDB works this way. New writes go into a small sorted in-memory **memtable** (plus an append-only log, so a crash can't lose them).

story.plain: A small sorted table in memory where new writes land first.
story.like: The pile on your desk before filing.

story.md: When the memtable fills, it's written out as an immutable sorted file called an **SSTable**. Later, background **compaction** merges small sorted files into bigger ones. This design is a **log-structured merge-tree** (LSM tree), described by O'Neil et al. in 1996. Every write becomes a cheap sequential append.

story.plain: A sorted file that is never edited after it's written.
story.like: A printed phone book: new editions replace it, nobody erases names.

story.md: In the obvious version, [[10|this line]] adds up how many items each insert has to shove aside. [[9-11|The in-place insert]] gets pricier as the list grows, because a typical key lands somewhere in the middle of a longer and longer list.

The LSM version never inserts into a big list. It piles keys up, and [[17-19|flushes a sorted run]] every 64. Once four runs exist, [[20-24|a tiny compaction]] merges them pairwise. Run the code and compare the two bars: the pile-first approach moves far fewer items. The second chart shows the sorted runs it leaves behind.

Fast writes cost you on reads. A key might be in the memtable or in any of several files, so a lookup may check them one by one. LevelDB can use **Bloom filters** to skip files that definitely lack the key. Compaction also rewrites data in the background. If your workload is mostly reads, or you need every lookup to touch one place, a plain sorted structure may suit you better.

fanout.q: How Twitter builds your timeline before you open the app
fanout.title: How Twitter builds your timeline before you open the app

story.md: You open Twitter and your home timeline is just *there*. No spinner, no waiting while the app goes hunting. But your timeline is a mix of posts from everyone you follow, and none of those people wrote their posts in the order you'll want to read them.

In the 2012 talk "Timelines at Scale", Twitter engineer Raffi Krikorian described the key fact: people **read** their timelines far more often than anyone **writes** a tweet. Whatever Twitter does, reading has to be fast.

When you open the app, look up everyone you follow, fetch each one's recent posts, merge them, sort them, and show the result. It's simple and always fresh. But it makes every *read* do the heavy work, and reads are the most common thing that happens. Follow 500 accounts and each app-open means 500 lookups, repeated for every user, all day.

Think of a **mailroom**. The slow way: each morning you walk around the building asking every colleague if they wrote anything for you. The fast way: when someone writes a note, they drop a copy in the mailbox of everyone who subscribes. In the morning your mailbox is already full. That's **fan-out on write**.

story.like: Mailing a copy to every subscriber the moment it's written.

story.md: Twitter kept each user's home timeline in an in-memory store (Redis), holding tweet IDs, so reading it is a quick lookup. There's a catch: an account with a huge follower count would trigger an enormous number of copies for one tweet. So for those accounts Twitter used a **hybrid**: skip the push, and merge their tweets into your timeline at read time.

ot.q: How Google Docs lets two people type in the same sentence
ot.title: How Google Docs lets two people type in the same sentence

story.md: Two people open the same Google Doc. The sentence says `the cat sat`. At the same instant, one of them adds a word in the middle and the other deletes the start. Neither waits for the other, and both screens must end up showing the **same** text.

Google's 2010 Drive blog series on the new Google Docs explained how it handles this. The hard part is that the edits cross paths on the network, so each person's copy changes before the other person's edit arrives.

Send each edit as "insert this text at position 4" or "delete 4 characters at position 0", and have everyone apply every edit exactly as sent. It breaks because a position only means something for the text it was written against. Once a delete lands first, "position 4" points at different letters. Each machine applies the same edits in a different order, and the copies **diverge**.

story.like: Two friends following the same directions from different starting corners.

story.md: Imagine you tell a friend "take the fourth door on the left", and before they arrive, someone removes the first four doors. Your directions are stale, so you have to rewrite them: "now it's the first door". Docs does this with every edit. Each edit is sent as an **operation**, and when two operations happen at the same time, each one is rewritten to account for the other.

story.md: That rewriting is called **operational transformation** (OT). A central server decides the order in which operations count. Each copy then transforms the incoming operation against the ones it didn't know about, for example shifting an insert's position if text was deleted before it, so every copy ends up identical.

It also leans on a central server to order operations. If you need simple data, such as a single settings value, or no server at all, a plain "last write wins" rule or a different approach may fit better.

Any shared editor faces the same question: what does "position 4" mean when the text under it has changed? Collaborative notes, code editors and whiteboards all have to answer it, whether they use OT or a different technique.

dropbox.q: How Dropbox uploads a 1 GB file in a second
dropbox.title: How Dropbox uploads a 1 GB file in a second

story.md: Picture a huge file in your Dropbox folder: a video, a design file, a big archive. You fix one tiny thing in the middle and press save. Dropbox now has to get that change onto its servers and your other devices.
People do this all day, with files that are enormous and edits that are small. If every tiny edit costs a full upload, sync feels slow and wastes a lot of network.

The simplest plan: whenever the file changes, upload the whole file again. It's easy to write and it works. But a 1-byte edit to a huge file sends the entire file, and uploading a file someone already stored sends it all over again. Almost all of those bytes are ones the server already has.

Think of a book copied page by page. Instead of mailing the whole book after fixing one typo, you tell the library which pages you have, and it says "we have all of those except page 48." You mail only page 48.

Dropbox's file format (described in its 2014 post "Streaming File Synchronization") works this way. Every file is split into **4 MB blocks**, and each block gets a **SHA-256** fingerprint. A file is then identified by its list of fingerprints, a **blocklist**. The server skips any block it already has.

story.plain: A fixed-size slice of a file, treated as one piece that can be stored or sent on its own.
story.like: One page of a book.

story.plain: A function that turns any chunk of data into a short fingerprint that is practically unique to that data.
story.like: A fingerprint for a chunk of bytes.

story.md: [[8|This line]] cuts the 400 KB file into 100 blocks of 4 KB, a scaled-down version of Dropbox's 4 MB blocks. [[9|The next line]] fingerprints each one. The `server` dict on [[11|line 11]] is keyed by those fingerprints, so asking "do you have this block?" is a single lookup.

The first sync sends all 100 blocks. Then [[25|the edit]] touches one block, so [[16-20|the sync loop]] sends exactly 1. The whole-file way would send all 400 KB again, while the smart way sends 4 KB. Syncing the original again sends 0, because the server has every block. That's the "already stored" case: nothing needs to travel.

You pay to hash every block and keep a lookup of what the server has, which is wasted effort for tiny files that fit in one block. In this toy, fixed-size slicing also means that inserting bytes near the start shifts every later block's contents and changes their hashes, so a plain edit-in-place is the happy case.

Hash-the-content-and-skip-what-you-have shows up in backup tools, in Git (which names things by content hashes), and in container image layers. Wherever big data changes a little, this idea saves the work.

import hashlib, random

BLOCK = 4096
random.seed(7)
original = random.randbytes(400 * 1024)

def blocklist(data):
    chunks = [data[i:i + BLOCK] for i in range(0, len(data), BLOCK)]
    return [(hashlib.sha256(c).hexdigest(), c) for c in chunks]

server = {}

def sync(data):
    sent = []
    for h, chunk in blocklist(data):
        if h in server:
            sent.append(0)
        else:
            server[h] = chunk
            sent.append(1)
    return sent

first = sync(original)
edited = bytearray(original)
edited[200000:200010] = b"CHANGED!!!"
edited = bytes(edited)
second = sync(edited)
copy = sync(original)

whole_kb = len(edited) // 1024
clever_kb = sum(second) * BLOCK // 1024
show([whole_kb, clever_kb], "KB sent: whole file vs new blocks")
show([first, second, copy], "rows: first upload, edit, same file again")
print(sum(first), sum(second), sum(copy))

kafka.title: LinkedIn's big idea: the humble log

story.md: Picture a big site like LinkedIn. Every click, page view and signup is an **event**. Lots of systems want those events: one sends emails, one builds analytics, one watches for abuse, and more keep showing up.
Wiring every producer to every consumer by hand turns into a tangle. This was the pain behind **Apache Kafka**, built at LinkedIn by Jay Kreps, Neha Narkhede and Jun Rao, and open-sourced in 2011.

Use a classic **queue**: a producer drops messages in, and once a service takes a message, it's deleted. That's fine for one reader. With two, they *compete* for messages, so email never sees what analytics took. A new fraud service arrives late and finds only leftovers, because the past is gone.
Think of a notebook where you only ever write at the bottom and never tear out pages. Each reader keeps their own bookmark. Nobody's reading affects anyone else, and a newcomer can open to page one.

That notebook is an append-only **log**. Kafka splits it into partitions, and keeps records for a retention period. Each consumer group tracks its own **offset**, so many readers go at their own pace and can replay from any point.

story.md: In [[10-13|the queue loop]], every pass removes one message and gives it to just one random service. The two bars add up to 30, so each service saw only a **slice** of the events. By the end, `queue` is empty.

A log keeps data, so it costs storage until retention drops old records. Readers must track their own offsets. Strict order holds only within one partition, not across the whole topic. If you just need one worker to handle each job exactly once, like a to-do list, a plain queue is simpler.

vclock.q: How Amazon’s cart never loses the thing you added
vclock.title: How Amazon's cart never loses the thing you added

story.md: Picture the shopping cart during a busy sale. Your cart lives on several servers, and a network hiccup cuts two of them off from each other. You tap "add to cart" on your phone, and your laptop adds something else. Both taps land on different servers.

Amazon's 2007 paper *Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store* describes a store that **always accepts writes**, even during network failures. Refusing your tap would be worse than a messy cart. So the hard question is what to do when the servers reconnect and disagree.

Keep whichever copy was saved last by the wall clock, a rule called last-writer-wins. It's simple, but it fails here. Both servers made a valid edit starting from the same cart, and neither saw the other's. Picking one throws the other away, so an item you added silently vanishes. Server clocks also drift, so "last" can be a guess.

Think of two coworkers editing printed copies of a shared shopping list. Each initials the page every time they change it. Later you can tell whether one copy already includes the other's changes, or whether they each changed it on their own. In Dynamo, every version carries a **vector clock**: a list of (server, counter) pairs recording who has edited it, and how many times.

story.plain: A small list of counters, one per server, attached to a value to record which edits it has seen.
story.like: Initials on a shared list, with a tally per person.

story.md: To compare two clocks, check every entry. If one clock is greater or equal in every entry, it **supersedes** the other: it already knows about those edits. If neither wins everywhere, the edits are **concurrent**. Dynamo keeps both versions, and the client **reconciles** them. For a cart, that means merging.

Dynamo gives up simplicity for availability. Conflicting versions must be stored and reconciled by the client, and a merged cart can't always tell a deliberate removal from a missing add, so deleted items can resurface. If you need one strict answer at all times, like a bank balance, don't use this approach.
The same idea of tracking causality and merging concurrent edits shows up in other systems that stay writable during network trouble, including collaborative editors and some distributed databases.
